title: Farfalle al salmone
subtitle: Bowtie pasta with smoked salmon, cream, and dill
excerpt: Farfalle al salmone pairs bowtie pasta with a quick cream sauce made with smoked salmon, dill, and a small amount of white wine. The salmon goes in off the heat so it warms through without toughening. This is the kind of pasta that takes 20 minutes and tastes far more considered than that.
sourceNotes: Italian-inspired home-cooking recipe. Smoked salmon cream pasta became popular across northern Italy and Italian-influenced cooking in the 1980s and 1990s. Method drawn from general Italian pasta-making tradition.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pasta shaped like bow ties or butterflies; the name means 'butterflies' in Italian; the pinched centre creates a slightly thicker middle that gives texture variation in each bite.

content.text: Farfalle al salmone is a cream pasta that needs almost no cooking: a shallot softened in butter, a splash of wine reduced, cream warmed through, then smoked salmon torn in at the end. The
catches the sauce in its folds. Keep the heat off the pan when the salmon goes in; it only needs warmth, not cooking.

items.prepNote: zest and a squeeze of juice

content.text: Cook {{pasta-dried}} of farfalle in a large pot of salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a mug of pasta water.

While the pasta cooks, melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a frying pan over medium heat. Add the shallots and cook for 4 minutes until soft. Pour in {{dry-white-wine}} of dry white wine and let it reduce by half. Add {{double-cream}} of cream and simmer for 3 minutes until the sauce coats a spoon. Remove from the heat. Add the lemon zest and a squeeze of juice.

Drain the pasta and toss with the cream sauce, adding pasta water to loosen. Fold in {{smoked-salmon}} of smoked salmon strips and the dill. Season with black pepper. The salmon will warm through in the residual heat; don't put the pan back on the hob. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Heat applied to the salmon after it was added.
items.fix: Always fold in the smoked salmon off the heat. It needs only the warmth of the pasta to heat through.

items.cause: Overcooked or too little pasta water added.
items.fix: Thin with pasta water, added a tablespoon at a time.

content.text: Smoked salmon cream pasta became popular in Italian restaurants outside Italy in the 1980s, pushed along by the wave of cream-based pasta dishes that Italian cooks brought to Britain and America. Inside Italy it is seen as a slightly foreign idea, though it is eaten in northern cities where cream sauces are common. Smoked salmon with dill is a combination that works wherever it is made.
